_comment: Voice-over lines for Bizzaro Bangalore. Generate with:
Two separate levers, per the pipeline notes: 'character' is fixed per
speaker and never changes between lines (that is the voice); 'delivery'
is per line (that is the take). Keeping them apart is what makes the
performance directable — without a delivery note every line in a scene
comes out in the same register regardless of what is happening in it.
Character descriptions deliberately say what NOT to do: left to itself
the model performs an accent rather than speaking in one.

narrator.character: a documentary narrator in the Vox explainer register — bright, articulate and conversational, speaking clean measured sentences with crisp consonants and a light forward momentum, as though walking the listener through evidence. He is dry rather than jokey, and trusts the material to be funny without selling it. Speak plainly and naturally — no announcer boom, no over-warm radio voice, no sing-song cadence, no theatrical emphasis, no caricature

passenger.character: a Bangalore software professional in his early thirties, speaking natural Indian English in an educated urban register — unhurried, fairly flat, the way someone talks when they are describing something that unsettled them and have not yet decided how they feel about it. Speak plainly and naturally — no performed or exaggerated accent, no theatrical shakiness, no comic timing, no caricature

correspondent.character: a television correspondent in his forties, speaking clean neutral English in the flat professional register of an interviewer who is not the subject of the piece. He asks his questions plainly and does not perform interest in the answers. No announcer boom, no warmth, no sing-song, no emphasis for effect

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Every day, thousands of auto rides begin in Bangalore. This is the story of the one that went right.
lines.delivery: matter-of-fact and unhurried, opening a case file; let the first sentence sit flat and ordinary, then land 'the one that went right' with a small dry lift — understated, never winking at the audience

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: No pause. No haggling. He simply put the meter down.
lines.delivery: deadpan and clipped, almost flat; the first two fragments land like items being ticked off a list, then a small beat before the last clause, stated as plain fact rather than a punchline

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: According to our survey, 91% of auto drivers refuse the Whitefield route outright.
lines.delivery: brisk and factual, reading a finding off a page; put the weight on the figure and on 'outright', and do not editorialise around either

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Of the 9% who accept — 96% still won't use the meter.
lines.delivery: same register, one notch drier; a small pause at the dash as though turning to the next column, then 'still' carrying a flicker of resignation without becoming a joke

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Which means, statistically... this shouldn't have happened at all.
lines.delivery: slower and quieter, the sentence a narrator says when the evidence has stopped adding up; a real pause after 'statistically', then the last clause flat and unhurried — no build, no emphasis on 'at all'

lines.speaker: correspondent
lines.text: Can you walk us through what happened?
lines.delivery: flat and procedural, an opening question asked a hundred times before; no curiosity in it at all

lines.speaker: passenger
lines.text: He put the meter down. Without even asking. He wasn't honking. He wasn't on the phone. He stopped at every single signal. He followed every rule.
lines.delivery: deadpan and even, recounting ordinary things as though each one were evidence of something wrong; a small pause between each item, building only by accumulation and never by rising pitch or emphasis

lines.speaker: passenger
lines.text: It almost felt like... I was in a parallel universe.
lines.delivery: quieter and drifting, as though replaying it; a real pause after 'It almost felt like', then the last phrase stated plainly as a fact rather than delivered as a punchline
